newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile approves building of controversial dam.
newsitem.headline: Chile approves building of controversial dam.

text.p: Chile's National Environmental Commission gave final approval on Monday for construction of a second, 570-megawatt dam on the Bio Bio River despite criticism from ecologists and Indians who will lose their land to the project.

The commission approved electric utility Endesa's environmental impact study for the dam in southern Chile on the condition that it carry out plans to relocate about 500 Pehuenche Indians whose ancestral lands will be flooded by the dam.
Endesa must also create a 9,400-acre (3,800-hectare) wildlife reserve nearby and accept independent auditing of the project, the commission said.
The $600 million project calls for a 508-foot (155-metre) high concrete wall spanning the upper reaches of the Bio Bio River in rainy, forested southern Chile.

Behind the dam, a 2,100-square-mile (5,440-sq-km) artificial lake will force the Pehuenche off their land and flood rare temperate rain forests and some of the world's best whitewater rafting stretches.
The dam's builders say Chile, with almost no oil of its own, needs Ralco and other big energy projects to guarantee the country's booming economic growth into the next century.

"Approval for Ralco confirms that this is an excellent project for the country's energy development," said a statement issued by Endesa. "Endesa has put its maximum effort into making Ralco cover all technical, economic and environmental aspects associated with it."

Endesa first submitted its environmental report last year but the commission effectively rejected it, saying the company's compensation and relocation plans for the Pehuenches were inadequate. Endesa rewrote the plan and resubmitted it.

Last year it finished building a smaller, 450-megawatt dam downstream known as Pangue, also criticised by environmentalists. Basic engineering work began last year on Ralco and full-scale construction can now begin, government officials said.

Criticism of the Ralco project reached the top echelons of one of its major financiers, the World Bank. Endesa in March paid back loans totalling $150 million from the World Bank's financial wing, the International Finance Corp, after the bank alleged Endesa was failing to live up to its environmental commitments in the dam projects.

In a letter addressed to Chile's Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat, World Bank president James Wolfensohn threatened in February to declare Endesa in default of its commitments under the loans' terms. Seeking to avoid financing complications, Endesa repaid the loans and got financing instead from a private German bank.
